meta.blurb: A hand touches Walter Hartright's arm on a dark road at midnight. It belongs to a woman dressed all in white, and she is running from someone. Soon a smiling count with pet white mice begins to plan something terrible.
meta.bible: Walter Hartright: a young drawing master and the hero; honest, brave, in love with Laura. The woman in white: Anne Catherick, a frail, frightened woman who escapes from an asylum and looks very like Laura; weak heart. Laura Fairlie: gentle, fair-haired heiress; becomes Lady Glyde; Mr Fairlie's niece. Marian Halcombe: Laura's half-sister, plain-faced, brave and clever; keeps a diary. Mr Fairlie: Laura's selfish, nervous uncle, owner of Limmeridge House. Sir Percival Glyde: a baronet in debt, who marries Laura for her money; secretly not the rightful heir to his name. Count Fosco: a huge, charming, clever Italian with white mice and a pet canary; the real villain; a traitor to a secret society. Madame Fosco: the Count's silent wife, Laura's aunt. Pesca: Walter's cheerful Italian friend, a member of the secret Brotherhood; Walter once saved his life. Mr Gilmore: the family lawyer. Mr Kyrle: the London lawyer Walter consults. Mrs Catherick: Anne's proud mother, who lives in Southampton and knows Percival's secret. Mrs Fairlie: Laura's late mother, buried at Limmeridge. Limmeridge House: the Fairlie home in Cumberland. Cumberland: the county. Blackwater Park: Sir Percival's gloomy house in Hampshire. Hampshire: the county. Welmingham: the village with the old church and its register. Southampton. London. Paris. Italy. Central America. The Brotherhood: a secret Italian society that punishes traitors. Voice and tone: a classic mystery told by several witnesses, with a rising sense of dread and then triumph; deaths are stated plainly, with no gore. The plot: Anne is dying and has Laura's face; the Count and Sir Percival swap them, so that Laura is shut up as Anne while Anne is buried as Laura; Walter, Marian and Laura prove the truth with a forged marriage register, a confession and a date.

B1B2: Walter Hartright, a young drawing teacher, was walking home on a moonlit road near London when a hand touched his shoulder. Behind him stood a pale woman dressed in white from head to foot.
The woman asked in a trembling voice for the road to London, and she seemed afraid of being followed. Walter walked beside her until they found a cab, and she thanked him with tears in her eyes.
A little later, two men asked Walter whether he had seen a woman in white. They told him that she had escaped from a hospital for the mind, and he felt a sudden chill.

Walter's friend Pesca, an Italian teacher whom Walter had once saved from drowning, found him work in the north of England. He was to teach drawing to two young ladies at Limmeridge House in Cumberland.
At Limmeridge House, Walter was met by Marian Halcombe, who was not pretty but who was clever and warm-hearted. She spoke to him plainly and quickly made him feel at home.
The owner of the house, Mr Fairlie, was a selfish man who spent his days among his pictures and coins. He pretended to be ill, and he hated any noise or trouble.
Laura Fairlie, the younger sister, was fair, gentle and shy, and Walter found it hard to look away from her. He began to teach the two ladies to draw, and the lessons went well.
As the weeks passed, Walter and Laura slowly fell in love, although neither of them said a word about it. Marian noticed the signs at once, and she began to worry for them both.
One morning, Laura received a letter with no name on it. It warned her not to marry Sir Percival Glyde, because he would bring her great sorrow.
Walter followed the trail of the letter to the churchyard, where he found the woman in white beside the grave of Laura's mother. She was Anne Catherick, and she looked very much like Laura.
Marian told Walter, kindly but firmly, that Laura had promised her dying father to marry Sir Percival. Walter must therefore leave Limmeridge, and he agreed with a heavy heart.
In the garden, Laura told Walter that she must keep her promise to her father, even though it was breaking her heart. He did not blame her, and he held her hand for the last time.

Marian pressed Walter's hand at the door, and the next morning he left Limmeridge, believing that he would never return. A few weeks later, he joined a team of explorers who were sailing to Central America.

Sir Percival Glyde arrived at Limmeridge, charming and polite, and he told Marian about Anne Catherick. He said that he had sent her to a hospital for her own good, and a letter from her mother seemed to prove it.
Mr Gilmore, the family lawyer, wrote the wedding papers and was worried by what he saw. If Laura died, her fortune would pass to Sir Percival, but Mr Fairlie did not care enough to object.
Laura married Sir Percival Glyde in the village church, looking pale but calm. The couple then travelled to Italy for six months, and Marian stayed at Limmeridge to wait for them.

When the couple returned, they lived at Blackwater Park, a gloomy old house in Hampshire, and Marian came to stay with them. Laura was thinner and sadder than before, and she did not speak about her marriage.
Count Fosco, a huge, smiling Italian, came to stay with his quiet wife, who was Laura's aunt. He kept white mice and a pet canary, and he spoke so charmingly that nobody could dislike him for long.
Marian wrote in her diary every night, and she admitted that the Count was the most dangerous man she had ever met. His intelligence frightened her, yet she could not help liking his gentleness.
One day Sir Percival put a paper in front of Laura and told her to sign it without reading it. Laura bravely refused, and her husband became very angry.
Marian suspected a plot, so one rainy night she climbed onto the roof to hear Percival and the Count talk. She heard enough to be afraid, but she got soaking wet and caught a serious fever.
Marian lay ill in bed for many days, and Laura nursed her with love. The Count visited often with kind words, and Laura did not notice that he was also watching them both.
While Marian slept, the Count read her secret diary from beginning to end. He even added a few polite lines to it, and so she knew that he had read every word.
Laura secretly met Anne Catherick at the old boathouse beside the lake. Anne said that she knew a terrible secret about Sir Percival, but before she could tell it, she heard a sound and ran away.
While Marian lay ill, Sir Percival and the Count told Laura a false story that sent her to London. Trusting them, she travelled to the city and was to spend a night at the Count's house.
Anne Catherick, whose heart had always been weak, was found ill in London and taken to the Count's house. There she died, and a doctor wrote down the cause of her death as an illness of the heart.

The Count and Sir Percival announced that Lady Glyde had died, and the body of Anne Catherick was buried at Limmeridge with Laura's name. Marian, still ill at Blackwater Park, heard the news with horror.
Meanwhile, the real Laura was taken to the asylum that Anne had escaped from, and the staff called her Anne Catherick. She told them her true name again and again, but nobody believed a word.
As soon as she could stand, Marian learned the truth and traced Laura to the asylum. She paid a nurse to help her, and together they brought Laura out safely.
Walter came back from Central America, tired and thin, and visited the grave of Lady Glyde to say goodbye. To his shock, he saw two women at the grave, and one of them was Laura.
Marian told Walter everything, and he promised to give Laura back her name. The three of them now lived together in cheap rooms in London, and Walter worked hard as an artist to pay for them.
A kind lawyer listened to the whole story, but he told Walter sadly that the law could not help without proof. The grave, the doctor's papers and the funeral all said that Laura was dead.
Walter remembered that Anne Catherick had known a terrible secret about Sir Percival. If he could find it, he might force the guilty men to tell the truth.
Walter travelled to the old church of Welmingham in Hampshire, where Sir Percival's parents had been married. The old clerk of the church showed him the great book in which marriages were written.
Walter copied the entry carefully and began to suspect that it was false. If the marriage had never taken place, Sir Percival had no right to his name or his land.

Walter visited Mrs Catherick, Anne's proud and cold mother, who lived in a neat house in Southampton. She would not tell the whole story, but her words showed that Sir Percival's secret was about his family.

One night at the opera, Walter's friend Pesca saw Count Fosco and turned white with fear. He explained that the Count was a spy who had betrayed a secret Italian brotherhood, and that its members would punish him.
Sir Percival learned that Walter knew his secret, and he decided to destroy the evidence at once. He hurried to the church at Welmingham and let himself into the little room where the book was kept.
In the dark, the lantern set fire to the room, and the flames spread faster than he expected. Walter and the villagers rushed to help, but the fire was too strong, and Sir Percival died there.
With Sir Percival dead, Walter went to Count Fosco's London house to face him. The Count received him calmly, offering tea and cakes, and listened with a polite smile.

Walter threatened to tell the secret Brotherhood where the Count was hiding, and the Count turned pale. He agreed to write a full confession of the plot in return for a few hours' start on his escape.
The Count fled to Paris, but members of the brotherhood soon found him. A few days later, his body was found in the Paris morgue, and everyone understood who had killed him.
In his confession, the Count gave the date on which Laura had left Blackwater Park. Walter saw that it came after the date on which, according to the papers, Lady Glyde had died.
Walter took Laura and Marian to Limmeridge, where the farmers and servants gathered round and knew her at once. Many of them cried, and they cheered when she said her own name.

Mr Fairlie complained loudly about all the noise and trouble, but he could not argue with the evidence. In the end, the proofs and the support of the villagers forced him to accept Laura as his true niece.
Walter did not forget Anne Catherick, who had warned them all. He arranged for her own name to be carved on the tomb at Limmeridge, so that she was remembered as herself.
After a decent time, Walter and Laura were married in the quiet village church where her sad story had begun. Marian wept with joy, and she said that she would never leave them.
Within a year, Walter and Laura had a baby son, and they were happier than they had ever been. Marian watched over him like a second mother, and she told the child stories every night.
Not long afterwards, Mr Fairlie died, and the little boy was now the heir to Limmeridge. He would one day be the master of the great house where his parents had first met.
Walter wrote down the whole story so that the world would know the truth about Laura. It began on a lonely road in the moonlight, and it ended in a happy home.
C1C2: Late one summer night, Walter Hartright, a young drawing master, was walking home to London along a lonely moonlit road when a hand suddenly touched his shoulder. He turned and saw, standing perfectly still in the moonlight, a pale woman dressed from head to foot in white. Nothing in the quiet landscape had warned him that she was there, and his heart beat hard against his ribs.

In a low and trembling voice, the stranger asked him the way to London, and as they walked together toward the city she begged him not to ask who she was. Her manner was gentle and educated, yet she glanced behind her at every sound like a hunted creature. At last Walter found her a cab, and she climbed into it with a murmur of thanks that was almost a sob.

A few minutes later, two men in a carriage stopped Walter and asked, with an air of authority, whether he had seen a woman dressed in white pass that way. They told him that she had escaped from an asylum where she was kept as a patient, and Walter, who had just helped her on her way, felt his conscience sting. Had he done a kindness to a frightened woman, or a wrong to a sick one?

Soon afterwards, Walter's friend Pesca, a lively Italian professor whose life Walter had once saved from the sea, came to him with a splendid offer of work. A rich gentleman in Cumberland, a Mr Fairlie of Limmeridge House, wanted a drawing master to teach his two nieces for a period of four months. Walter, who needed money and a change of scene, accepted without a moment's delay.

At Limmeridge House, Walter was welcomed by Marian Halcombe, a tall dark young woman whose face was not beautiful but whose eyes shone with intelligence and humour. She spoke with a frankness that startled him and charmed him in the same moment, and within an hour he felt that he had made a friend. Her half-sister Laura, she explained, was the true mistress of the house, and would join them presently.

The master of the house was Mr Fairlie, Laura's uncle, a pale and selfish gentleman who passed his days among rare prints and old coins and complained constantly of his nerves. He was convinced that the smallest noise might kill him, and he shrank from any difficulty as if it were an infection. Everyone in the house had learned to manage him by telling him as little as possible.

Laura Fairlie proved to be a slender, fair-haired girl of great sweetness, with a shy gentleness of manner that made every word she spoke sound like a kindness. Walter began his lessons the next morning, and he soon found that his eyes returned to her face far more often than the work required. He told himself that it was merely the pleasure of teaching a talented pupil.

As the weeks passed, the quiet intimacy of the lessons deepened into something that neither Walter nor Laura could name, and neither dared to speak of it aloud. Marian, who missed nothing, saw how often their eyes met over the drawings and how long their hands lingered on the paper. She grew anxious, for she alone knew that Laura was promised to another man.

One morning an unsigned letter reached Limmeridge, warning Laura in urgent words that she must never marry Sir Percival Glyde, the gentleman to whom she had long been engaged. Marian read it twice with a growing sense of dread, for the writer plainly knew a great deal about the family and plainly meant every word. She decided that she would not rest until she discovered who had sent it, and why.

Walter's search for the writer of the letter led him one evening to the churchyard, where, beside the white marble tomb of Laura's mother, he found the strange woman of the moonlit road. She was Anne Catherick, a frail and fearful creature who had once been cared for by Mrs Fairlie and who had never forgotten her kindness. Seeing her face clearly for the first time, Walter was shocked by how much it resembled Laura's.

Marian took Walter aside and told him, with great gentleness, that Laura had given her dying father a solemn promise to marry Sir Percival Glyde and could not break it without disgrace. Walter, whose love was now as plain to Marian as it was painful to himself, understood that he could not stay a day longer under the same roof. He accepted her judgement with a heavy heart, and even thanked her for her honesty.

In the garden at dusk, Laura told Walter in a trembling voice that she must keep the promise she had made to her father, even though it was breaking her heart. Walter, who had no right to ask her for anything, answered that he honoured her for it, and the two stood together in silence while the light faded from the sky. Then he pressed her hand for the last time, and walked away across the darkening lawn without once looking back.

Marian pressed his hand at the door with a look that told him how much she understood, and the next morning Walter left Limmeridge, believing that he would never see it again. A few weeks later he joined an expedition of explorers and scholars bound for Central America, hoping that distance and danger might cure his heart. The great adventure would take him far from England, and from every friend he loved, for many months.

Sir Percival Glyde proved to be an elegant, well-mannered gentleman who bore the anonymous letter with perfect calm and offered to explain it at once. He told Marian that the writer was a poor deranged woman named Anne Catherick, whom he had himself placed in an asylum out of kindness to her mother, and a letter from Mrs Catherick seemed to confirm every word. Marian, relieved and reassured, persuaded Laura that the wedding might safely go forward, and for a while the matter was closed.

Mr Gilmore, the family lawyer, drew up the marriage settlement with growing unease, for its terms were far more generous to the bridegroom than a careful guardian would have liked. If Laura were to die, nearly all of her large fortune would pass to her husband, yet Mr Fairlie, too idle to quarrel, refused to ask for any change. The lawyer departed with a heavy conscience and a silent wish that the young bride might be well protected.

Laura kept her promise, and in the little village church she became Lady Glyde, pale and quiet and obedient to the end of the service. The newly married pair left almost at once for a long tour of Italy, which was expected to last six months, and Marian, who loved her sister more than anyone, was left behind with an aching heart. The great house at Limmeridge, without its young mistress, had never felt so large or so empty.

On their return from Italy the couple settled at Blackwater Park, a vast, gloomy house in Hampshire whose empty rooms and overgrown lake seemed to soak up any cheerfulness. Marian came to stay at once, and she was dismayed to find Laura thinner, paler and strangely unwilling to speak about her husband. Sir Percival himself was now often short-tempered and restless, as though some worry were gnawing at him.

Count Fosco, a vast and smiling Italian of great culture, arrived with his pale and silent wife, who was Laura's aunt, and at once seemed to fill the whole house. He carried white mice in his pockets, kept a canary that perched on his finger, and spoke on every subject with a charm that made even unwilling listeners lean forward. Marian, though she tried to resist him, found herself fascinated by the man and more than a little afraid of him.

Every night Marian recorded the day in her diary, and she confessed in its pages that she had never met a more dangerous man than the smiling Count. His intelligence, she wrote, was matched only by his coolness, and she was ashamed to find that even she could not help liking him. It was a warning that she would later wish, with all her heart, that she had trusted more completely.

One morning Sir Percival laid a document before Laura, covered the writing with his hand and ordered her to sign her name without so much as reading it. Laura, for once finding a spark of courage, refused to put her name to a page that she was not allowed to see, and her husband's face grew dark with fury. Only the arrival of the Count, with his soothing voice, prevented a more violent scene.

Convinced that some plot was being laid, Marian crept out on a wet and windy night and climbed onto the roof above the library to listen to the two men talking below. She learned enough to confirm her worst fears about Laura's money and her husband's debts, but she stayed too long in the cold rain and was soon burning with a dangerous fever. Within a day she could hardly lift her head from the pillow, and the house grew very quiet around her.

For many days Marian lay helpless with fever, and Laura, forgetting her own troubles, nursed her with a devotion that no servant could have equalled. The Count called every morning with soft words and sympathetic looks, and neither woman suspected that his visits had another purpose than kindness. All the while, in the quiet house, the plot against Laura was growing steadily and unseen.

While Marian lay delirious, the Count calmly took her private diary, read it from beginning to end and, with his usual impudence, wrote a polite and flattering note on its final page. When she was well enough to read it, she understood that the man she feared had known her every thought, and she could not decide whether she was more angry or more afraid. His note praised her courage, and it ended with a bow that she found chillingly sincere.

Meanwhile Laura, who had long wished to meet the woman who had warned her, slipped away to the old boathouse beside the lake and found Anne Catherick waiting there in her white dress. Anne claimed that she knew a terrible secret about Sir Percival, one that could destroy him if it were ever told, but before she could say more, she heard a footstep and fled into the trees. Laura was left alone, her heart pounding, with a promise of more to come.

While Marian was still too ill to leave her bed, Sir Percival and the Count told Laura an elaborate and plausible story that persuaded her to go to London. Trusting them completely, she packed a small bag and travelled to the city, where she was to rest for a night at the Count's house. It was the last journey that she would ever make under her own name, though she could not know it.

Anne Catherick, whose heart had always been weak, was found in London, ill and exhausted, and the Count's agents carried her to his house as though she were an honoured guest. There, a few days later, she died of her heart condition, and a doctor was called to sign the usual papers. Nobody mentioned how closely the dead woman resembled Lady Glyde, although everyone in the house had noticed it.

The Count and Sir Percival announced that Lady Glyde had died suddenly in London, and the body of poor Anne Catherick was carried to Limmeridge and buried in the family churchyard beneath Laura's name. Her fortune, as the marriage settlement had arranged, passed to her husband at once. Marian, still weak at Blackwater Park, heard the news and felt the whole world turn dark around her.

Meanwhile the true Laura, confused and unwell, was taken in secret to the very asylum from which poor Anne had escaped, and the staff were told that she was the runaway patient, Anne Catherick. Again and again she insisted that she was Lady Glyde, and again and again the attendants smiled sadly, for they had been warned that this was exactly what the poor creature would say. Her likeness to Anne, which had once seemed a curiosity, had become a prison.

As soon as she could stand, Marian discovered the truth, and with courage that would have done credit to a general she traced Laura to the asylum, refusing to believe in her death. By means of a bribe to one of the nurses, she contrived to get her sister out of the building and into a carriage, and the two clung to each other in the darkness. Laura, thin and dazed but alive, was beside her again, and for Marian that was enough to begin again.

Walter returned from Central America, worn out by fever and danger, and made his way at once to the churchyard at Limmeridge, where he read with horror the name of Laura, Lady Glyde, carved on a new marble tomb. As he stood there, two veiled women approached from the village, and when one of them lifted her veil, he found himself looking at Laura, thinner and paler but unmistakably alive. The shock was so great that, for a moment, he could neither speak nor move.

Marian told him everything, and Walter, listening with white lips, swore a silent vow to restore Laura to her name, her home and her place in the world. The three of them moved into cheap and humble rooms in London, where Walter worked tirelessly at his drawings to pay for their food, and Laura slowly recovered her strength. They were poor and alone, and the law, as they soon learned, believed that she was dead.

A kindly lawyer, Mr Kyrle, heard the extraordinary story with real sympathy, but he told Walter that the law could do nothing without proof, and every official paper declared that Laura was dead. The gravestone, the doctor's certificate and the record of the funeral were all against them, and nothing but strong evidence could undo such a chain of lies. Walter left the office determined to find the weak link in that chain, whatever it might cost him.

Walter remembered that Anne Catherick had hinted at a terrible secret that could destroy Sir Percival, and he understood that this secret might be the key to everything. If he could discover it, he reasoned, the guilty men would have to bargain, and Laura's name might be saved in the process. It was a faint hope, but it was the only path that was open to him.

Following his one clue, Walter travelled to the old church of Welmingham in Hampshire, where Sir Percival's parents were supposed to have been married, and he found the elderly parish clerk willing to talk about old times. The clerk led him into the vestry, where the great register of marriages was kept in an iron chest, and he showed him the page. Walter studied the entry slowly, with a sense that something about it was not quite right.

Walter copied the entry word for word, for he had begun to suspect that it was a forgery, written into the book long after the day it claimed to record. If the marriage it described had never taken place, he realised, then Sir Percival Glyde was not the rightful heir to his name or his estate. The thought was so large that he could hardly breathe as he walked out into the churchyard.

Walter then called upon Mrs Catherick, Anne's mother, a proud and hard-faced woman who lived in a neat house at Southampton and who had never forgiven the world for her troubles. She refused to tell him the whole story, and she took pleasure in his disappointment, but her careless words gave him all he needed to confirm his guess. Sir Percival, it was clear, had no right to the name and the fortune that he enjoyed.

At the opera one evening, Pesca caught sight of Count Fosco across the theatre and turned as white as paper, trembling like a man who has seen a ghost. He confided to Walter that he belonged to a secret Italian brotherhood, that the Count was a spy who had betrayed its members, and that the brotherhood never forgot a traitor. The Count, glancing up, recognised Pesca too, and from that moment his famous composure began to crack.

When Sir Percival learned that Walter had been asking questions, he understood that everything was in danger, and he resolved to destroy the evidence once and for all. Under cover of darkness he hurried to the church at Welmingham, let himself into the vestry with a key that he had secretly obtained, and set down his lantern beside the great iron chest. He meant to cut the guilty page from the register and burn it before the morning.

In the dark, his lantern set fire to the vestry, and the flames spread through the old wood faster than he could have imagined, shutting him in the room with the register he had come to destroy. Walter and a crowd of villagers ran to the church at the first red glow, and they fought desperately to break down the door, but the heat drove them back. When at last the fire was put out, Sir Percival Glyde was found dead among the ashes, and the secret he had tried to hide was out.

With Sir Percival dead, Walter determined to face the Count himself, and he climbed the stairs of the large London house where the great man now lived with his wife and his pets. Fosco received him with perfect courtesy, offered him refreshments, and heard him out with a polite smile, as if the whole matter were a delightful puzzle. Only the quick movement of his plump fingers betrayed that he was thinking very fast.

Walter then told him plainly that he knew the Count's old connection with the brotherhood, and that Pesca could lead its avengers to him within a day. The great man, white to the lips, agreed to write out a full and truthful account of the plot against Laura, on condition that Walter allowed him a few hours to leave England. Fosco wrote for a long time, with his usual elegance, and he seemed to enjoy telling the tale of his own cleverness.

The Count left London that same night and fled to Paris, but the long arm of the brotherhood reached him before he could settle into his new life. A few days later his body was discovered in the Paris morgue, where the unclaimed dead are laid out for the public, and nobody who knew his history had any doubt about who had killed him. So ended the career of the most brilliant and the most dangerous man that Walter had ever known.

Walter studied the Count's pages with the greatest care, and among the details he found a date that struck him like a blow: the day on which Laura had left Blackwater Park for London. It was a day after the one given in the doctor's certificate as the date of Lady Glyde's death, so Laura could not possibly have died on the day claimed. The certificate, and with it the whole story, was false, and Walter now held the evidence to prove it.

Walter brought Laura and Marian back to Limmeridge, where the old tenants and servants, who had known her from childhood, crowded around her and recognised her at once. Many wept openly, and when she spoke her own name aloud in the village square, they cheered until the windows shook. No court in England could have asked for stronger witnesses than those honest and joyful faces.

Mr Fairlie, shrinking in his chair, complained bitterly of the noise and the trouble, and he tried for a time to treat the whole business as a clever invention. In the end, however, the evidence, the dates and the united voices of his own tenants were too much even for him, and he declared in a weak voice that Laura was indeed his niece. Laura Fairlie, so long dead in the eyes of the law, was alive again at last.

Walter did not forget the poor, frightened woman whose death had been used so cruelly, and whose first warning had set the whole story in motion. He arranged that the false inscription on the marble tomb at Limmeridge should be replaced, so that Anne Catherick might at last be remembered under her own name. It seemed to him a small act of justice, but one that Laura, with her tender heart, deeply appreciated.

After a decent interval, Walter and Laura were married in the same quiet church where she had once given her hand to another man. Marian, who had stood by them through the darkest days, wept for joy, and she declared that no power on earth would ever separate her from her dear sister. It was the kind of ending that, a year before, none of them would have dared to dream.

A little later, a baby son was born to Walter and Laura, and the household that had known such sorrow now rang with laughter and song. Marian, who adored the child, watched over him like a second mother, and she was never happier than when she was telling him stories by the fire. Walter often looked at the three of them and felt that every danger he had faced had been worth it.

Mr Fairlie, who had spent his whole life guarding his comfort, died not long afterwards, and it was found that Walter and Laura's little boy was the heir to the great house of Limmeridge. In this way, the young drawing master who had once arrived in Cumberland with nothing but a box of paints had become the father of its future master. Fate, it seemed, had a sense of humour as well as a sense of justice.

Walter set down the whole story in his own words, so that the truth about Laura might never again be doubted, and so that every person who had helped her might be remembered. It had begun on a lonely road beneath the moon, with a pale stranger and a few trembling words, and it ended in a house full of laughter. He laid down his pen and went out to join his family in the garden, where the evening light was falling softly on the grass.
